extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, and policymakers interested in the role of the press and public opinion in democratic societies
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria from Lippmann's discussion of democracy and the press to evaluate how newspapers serve public opinion, including economic incentives, informational functions, legal limits, and measures of governmental performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate government by processes and results, not origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic fallacy has been its preoccupation with the origin of government rather than with the processes and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a government solely by the legitimacy of how power is derived (voting/representation); instead assess how power is actually exercised and whether it produces beneficial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of living as criteria for government
rubrics_metrics.description: The criteria which you then apply to government are whether it is producing a certain minimum of health, of decent housing, of material necessities, of education, of freedom, of pleasures, of beauty...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, objective standards of citizens' wellbeing (health, housing, material necessities, education, freedom, pleasures, beauty) as measures of governmental quality; the more exact and objective these criteria, the better political decisions relate to people's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain recording and objective measurement (audits) of officials' acts
rubrics_metrics.description: We can steadily increase our real control over these acts by insisting that all of them shall be plainly recorded, and their results objectively measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on transparent record-keeping and performance measurement (audits) of public officials and industrial directors so that decisions and outcomes are visible and evaluable; developing such standards and audits is an ongoing project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press must make the invisible world visible
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is the chief means of contact with the unseen environment... political thought might come to grips with the problem of how to make the invisible world visible to the citizens of a modern state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the press by its capacity to gather and present technical, complex, and distant information that citizens cannot observe directly; effective democracy requires this informational function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech alone is insufficient without organized information production
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberty in this sense does not guarantee public opinion in the modern world... the truth about distant or complex matters is not self-evident, and the machinery for assembling information is technical and expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that protecting civil liberties (free expression) is necessary but not sufficient; systems and resources for producing reliable information are required for public opinion to be well-formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic incentives and advertiser influence on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is... an asset only when it can be sold to the advertiser... A newspaper which angers those whom it pays best to reach through advertisements is a bad medium for an advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how advertiser demands and the need to monetize circulation shape editorial choices; newspapers will tend to respect the point of view of the buying public because advertisers pay for access to that audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty as a source of editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper that can really depend upon the loyalty of its readers is as independent as a newspaper can be... A body of readers who stay by it through thick and thin is a power greater than any which the individual advertiser can wield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure independence partly by the strength and loyalty of readership: stable, committed readers reduce vulnerability to advertiser pressure and increase editorial freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are judged by handling of news that affects readers personally
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us tends to judge a newspaper... by its treatment of that part of the news in which we feel ourselves involved... If the newspaper gives a satisfactory account of that which we think we know, ... it is fairly certain to be immune from violent criticism by us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect readers to evaluate accuracy and fairness primarily on local/personal matters they can check; distant or complex reporting will face less direct correction from the general reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal recourse for misreporting is limited to aggrieved parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The general reader of a newspaper has no standing in law if he thinks he is being misled by the news. It is only the aggrieved party who can sue for slander or libel...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that defamation law gives private remedies to those personally harmed but does not offer a collective legal remedy for misleading general news; this shapes accountability mechanisms for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of entertainment and local diary material to secure circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper takes to itself a variety of other features, all primarily designed to hold a body of readers together... scandal and crime, sports, pictures, actresses, advice to the lovelorn... not because publishers and editors are interested in everything but news, but because they have to find some way of holding on to that alleged host of passionately interested readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newsroom content choices with the recognition that non-political, entertainment, and local-interest features are central tools to build and retain readership and thereby sustain the paper economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted circulation (quality vs mass) influences editorial strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The kind of circulation which the advertiser will buy depends on what he has to sell. This may be 'quality' or 'mass.' ... the paper which goes into the homes of the fairly prosperous is by and large the one which offers most to the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify newspapers by the advertiser-desired audience they pursue; 'quality' audiences and 'mass' audiences lead to different content mixes and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealed funding via advertising undermines transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The public pays for the press, but only when the payment is concealed... He will pay directly to advertise. And he will pay indirectly for the advertisements of other people, because that payment, being concealed in the price of commodities is part of an invisible environment that he does not effectively comprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the lack of transparent funding flows (advertising hidden in consumer prices) as a factor that distances readers from understanding who finances news and whose interests are served.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undervaluation of straight reporting reduces professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting, which theoretically constitutes the foundation of the whole institution, is the most poorly paid branch of newspaper work... By and large, able men go into it only by necessity or for experience... straight reporting is not a career that offers many great rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the institutional strength of journalism by the pay, prestige, and career prospects for reporters; low rewards impede development of corporate traditions, professional norms, and high standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert intermediaries to keep public images realistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The only prospect... is that each of us in his own sphere will act more and more on a realistic picture of the invisible world, and that we shall develop more and more men who are expert in keeping these pictures realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and foster the role of specialized experts, journalists, and institutions who translate complex information into reliable images for citizens; democratic governance depends on such intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal for independent tribunals to sift charges of untruthfulness and unfairness
rubrics_metrics.description: It might, however, be a good thing if there were competent tribunals, preferably not official ones, where charges of untruthfulness and unfairness in the general news could be sifted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mechanisms beyond legal suits—such as independent, non-governmental tribunals or press councils—to adjudicate complaints about accuracy and fairness in general news, improving accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expectation of gratis truth undermines news funding
rubrics_metrics.description: We expect the newspaper to serve us with truth however unprofitable the truth may be... Nobody thinks for a moment that he ought to pay for his newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the cultural expectation that news should be cheap or free constrains revenue models and can lead to underinvestment in costly newsgathering necessary for truthful reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial alignment with local publishers' social milieu
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers are themselves usually members of these urban communities, and honestly see the world through the lenses of their associates and friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the social and class position of publishers and editors when evaluating potential biases and the framing of news; local social networks shape editorial outlooks.
